correctness.rationale: Legendre digit sums allow removal of the common p^t from upper, lower and complementary arguments. Write k=p^(a−v)j with p∤j, so its valuation is that of the coefficient C(up^v,uj). The exact minimization at level a is over the disjoint primitive-index levels 1≤v≤a. The first v positions in uj+u(p^v−j)=up^v each carry: the first digit is nonzero in each summand and sums to zero modulo p, and at each subsequent position an incoming carry cannot yield zero without another carry. Equivalently, C(up^v,uj)=(up^v/(uj))C(up^v−1,uj−1) gives valuation at least v. The level-one candidate j=1 has valuation c≥1, so levels v≥c cannot improve that minimum, yielding cutoff R=max(1,c−1), not a claim of least cutoff. Lower exponent gcd valuations can also be recovered from the upper row at exponent R by using only lower indices with k divisible by p^(R−a). Only level 1 can give valuation 1, and Legendre there gives the stated expression. For p=2 it is the digit sum of odd u, equal to 1 exactly when u=1; for p>u, (p−1)u=(u−1)p+(p−u) has digit sum p−1. A separate manual check gives D_1(11,2)=3 and D_2(11,2)=2, the latter using the valuation-2 coefficient C(44,11) and both level lower bounds. The supplied checks were inspected but not run; finite recorded output is corroboration only.

evidence: Wu Theorem 2 assumes a prime-power m and restricted prime factors of C(mn,m); Theorem 3 gives the full gcd for m=2. The 1985 publisher abstract describes consecutive terms in a Pascal row. The non-coprime indices abstract describes a larger index family, not the same selection.
broader_coverage.reasoning: Selecting a subset of the indices of a known gcd can increase its valuations, so the unrestricted, consecutive or non-coprime family does not determine this minimum. A stronger exact-family theorem for carefully selected m does not imply certification at arbitrary u.

evidence: Kummer/Legendre give individual coefficient valuations. claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: The classical valuation tools justify the ingredients, but do not state the upper limit on the number of levels one must inspect or the equivalence to a single level for valuation one. The prime-power result concerns precisely the slice where the remaining factor u is 1 and cannot handle strict drops at u=11 or u=39.

value.rationale: For a fixed multiplier the proof removes dependence on a potentially arbitrarily large prime-power exponent in a natural restricted gcd problem. The primitive-level decomposition explains actual strict valuation drops and makes a nontrivial finite cutoff and complete valuation-one test possible. This is not a fresh calculation of the classical full-row gcd.
residual_risks: The cutoff need not be minimal and concerns only the selected prime, not all factors of the gcd.
